title: Prompt Engineering Notes
section: Claude: The prompting playbook [Margot van Laar]
text:
Claude: The prompting playbook [Margot van Laar]

Use XML tags to structure prompts for clarity and consistency.
Be clear and direct in your instructions, avoiding ambiguity.
Curate the information you provide to the model, focusing on relevant details.
Start with an evaluation suite before changing any prompt. Cover three types of cases: control cases (should always pass), edge cases (previous failures you want to prevent), and capability-boundary cases (when the model should escalate, refuse, or hand off to a human).
Apply prompt hygiene first: remove redundant or outdated content (e.g., website copy, cookie notices, “you are a human” statements) and separate role, guidelines, policy, tone, and data with clear structure (XML tags work especially well).
If a human cannot distinguish guidelines from policy from data while reading the prompt, the model almost certainly cannot either.
Create an explicit output contract (e.g., wrap the response in specific XML tags) and reinforce it at the harness level with stop sequences so the model knows exactly when to stop.
Treat old defensive patches as technical debt. Instructions written for a previous model’s weaknesses often cause new failures (including the opposite of hallucination: withholding information the model actually has). Version-control the reason for every instruction so you can remove it when the model improves.
Instructions do not add capability. Telling the model “calculate correctly” or “this is critical” does not improve arithmetic. Give it a reliable tool (with proper API declaration, schema, and implementation) instead, and let the model reason about when to use it.
When the model must make a trade-off (e.g., escalate a billing error vs. keep handling the conversation), state both sides of the cost/benefit clearly. Stronger models will otherwise overfit to whichever side you emphasize.
When building a new agentic system, optimize the combination of model × prompt × harness (tools, structured outputs, stop sequences, adaptive thinking, etc.), not the prompt in isolation.
For multi-step or constrained generation tasks, prefer a generate → evaluate → repair loop with several simple, focused prompts over one giant monolithic prompt.

title: Prompt Engineering Notes
section: Tina Huang: Google’s 9 Hour AI Prompt Engineering Course In 20 Minutes Tina Huang
text:
Tina Huang: Google’s 9 Hour AI Prompt Engineering Course In 20 Minutes Tina Huang

Use the five-step TCREI framework for every prompt: Task (what to do, plus persona + desired format), Context (background, audience, constraints), References (examples / few-shot), Evaluate (does the output meet the need?), Iterate (refine and retry). Mnemonic: “Tiny crabs ride enormous iguanas” (or Google’s “Thoughtfully Create Really Excellent Inputs”).
Always be iterating (“ABI”). Four practical iteration methods: (1) revisit the full TCREI framework and add missing pieces, (2) break long prompts into shorter, clearer sentences, (3) rephrase or try an analogous task, (4) add constraints to narrow the solution space.
Specify persona and output format early in the Task step—they dramatically improve relevance and usability.
Provide rich context and concrete references/examples; more relevant detail almost always beats a sparse prompt.
Multimodal prompting follows the same principles: clearly state what the inputs are (text, image, audio, etc.) and what form the output should take.
Watch for hallucinations and inherited biases. Keep a human-in-the-loop: always verify important outputs before using or sharing them. Avoid feeding sensitive data into public models.
For everyday work: build and maintain a personal prompt library of reusable, high-performing prompts (emails, summaries, tables, brainstorming, etc.).
For data analysis & presentations: prompt for insights, formulas, patterns, and slide structures, but treat generated numbers and claims with extra scrutiny.
Advanced techniques:

Prompt chaining — break a complex goal into a sequence of linked prompts, feeding each output into the next (e.g., manuscript → summaries → taglines → full marketing plan).
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) — explicitly ask the model to show its step-by-step reasoning.
Tree-of-Thought (ToT) — ask the model to explore multiple reasoning paths / options in parallel and evaluate them.
Meta-prompting — ask the AI to help write or improve the prompt itself when you are stuck.

Create lightweight AI agents by defining a clear persona, context, conversation rules, and a stop phrase. Two useful patterns: simulation agents (role-play / practice interviews) and expert-feedback agents (critique pitches, drafts, etc.).
Responsible use checklist: verify accuracy, check for bias, protect sensitive information, and treat AI as a collaborator rather than an infallible authority.

title: Prompt Engineering Notes
section: DeepLearningAI: Prompt Engineering for Developers DeepLearningAI Andrew Ng
text:
DeepLearningAI: Prompt Engineering for Developers DeepLearningAI Andrew Ng

Treat the AI like a smart, highly motivated fresh college graduate who knows nothing about you yet. Give it the context a new hire would need (documents, screenshots, project trackers, voice memos, past work) instead of short Google-style queries.
Provide rich, relevant context. Modern models can handle very large context windows (~750k words). Start a new chat for unrelated topics so stale context does not degrade performance.
Understand the three knowledge sources and when to use each:

Pre-trained knowledge (good for general/common facts; limited by training cutoff and data frequency).
Web search (real-time info; note that the main model often only sees summaries produced by a helper model, not the full pages).
Deep research / agentic modes (many parallel searches, iterative evaluation, synthesized cited reports—for complex, multi-source questions).

Defeat sycophancy (the model’s tendency to please you). Ask neutral questions that do not hint at your preferred answer. Use objective rubrics with clear scoring criteria before asking for a score or judgment.
Use AI as a thought partner, not a one-shot answer machine. For brainstorming: supply context → request multiple options → give feedback → iterate. Feedback on options often matters more than more upfront context.
Prefer progressive outlining for writing: outline → critique/refine the outline → expand to bullet points → iterate → only then draft full text. This avoids generic “AI slop” and makes structural changes easy.
For complex reasoning tasks, explicitly cue longer thinking (“think hard,” “ultra think,” or enable reasoning/thinking mode). Classic “think step by step” is largely obsolete on modern models.
When editing or evaluating work, give the model a clear rubric first; then ask it to apply the rubric. This produces more objective, useful feedback.
Leverage multimodal and tool-using capabilities: upload images/files, generate images, analyze data/spreadsheets, write and run code, and build simple websites/apps with natural-language instructions (no coding background required).
Desktop/agentic AI apps can explore local files (with permission). Best practice: state the overall task, let the model propose a plan, then approve execution.
Power-user habits: iterate aggressively, request multiple options, keep conversations focused, verify important claims (especially from search/deep research), and continually give the model harder, more context-rich tasks.

title: Prompt Engineering Notes
section: The Prompt Is Not the Architecture — But It Still Governs How the System Reasons (Interesting Engineering, 2026-05-23)
text:
The Prompt Is Not the Architecture — But It Still Governs How the System Reasons (Interesting Engineering, 2026-05-23)

The prompt is not the architecture, but it still governs how the system reasons. Architecture (harness, tools, gates, loops, meta-observation) determines what the system can see and do; the prompt/spec governs reasoning style and action selection.
Prompting has fragmented into four distinct disciplines (per Nate B Jones). Most people only practice the first:

Prompt craft (structure, XML, role, output format)
Context engineering (domain facts, background, memory tiers)
Intent engineering (state the desired outcome / what “good” looks like, not just the task)
Specification engineering (acceptance criteria, constraints, ordering, trade-off framings)

A strong single structured system prompt that embeds all four disciplines can outperform multi-agent swarms on single-turn, well-scoped document tasks (H2 scored α = 1.000; five-agent swarm scored 0.625).
Brownfield (existing, messy production systems) vs greenfield (clean-slate tasks) matters. Complex constraint-satisfaction or continuous operational systems usually need correction loops or adaptive architectures, not just a bigger prompt.
Generate → Evaluate → Repair (GER) loops are often more reliable and cheaper than relying solely on the model’s adaptive/extended thinking for hard constraint tasks.
Instructions do not add capability. Arithmetic, deterministic calculations, and similar tasks should be offloaded to tools/functions rather than instructed in natural language.
Legacy defensive patches written for older, weaker models can actively harm performance on newer models (e.g., causing the model to withhold information it actually has). Audit and remove outdated guardrails on model upgrades.
Prefer trade-off framings over rigid binary rules for judgment calls (state both sides of the cost/benefit). Keep hard binary checks only at verification gates.
Use API-level stop sequences / output contracts (not just prompt text) to enforce structured endings and reduce padding or runaway generation.
Ordering of instructions matters: place steps in the same sequence a competent human would reason through the problem.
The “35-minute wall”: once agents run autonomously for roughly that long without check-ins, chat-style prompting assumptions break. Everything critical must be pre-encoded in the specification before launch.
Intent engineering (closing the loop between predicted outcomes and actual results, then calibrating future behavior) is often the missing operational discipline, not a pure engineering problem.
Meta-harness / meta-observation layers that read execution traces across runs can surface failure modes that pure pre-specification cannot anticipate.
Architecture choices should match the problem type: high-density single prompt for greenfield document tasks; correction loops + tools + meta-observation for brownfield continuous operations.

At its core, Agentic AI is a type of AI that’s all about autonomy. This means that it can make decisions, take actions, and even learn on its own to achieve specific goals. It’s kind of like having a virtual assistant that can think, reason, and adapt to changing circumstances without needing constant direction. Agentic AI operates in four key stages:


Perception: AI agents gather and process data from various sources, such as sensors, databases and digital interfaces. This involves extracting meaningful features, recognizing objects or identifying relevant entities in the environment.
Reasoning: A large language model acts as the orchestrator, or reasoning engine, that understands tasks, generates solutions and coordinates specialized models for specific functions like content creation, visual processing or recommendation systems. This step uses techniques like retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to access proprietary data sources and deliver accurate, relevant outputs.
Action: By integrating with external tools and software via application programming interfaces, agentic AI can quickly execute tasks based on the plans it has formulated. Guardrails can be built into AI agents to help ensure they execute tasks correctly. For example, a customer service AI agent may be able to process claims up to a certain amount, while claims above the amount would have to be approved by a human.
Learning: Agentic AI continuously improves through a feedback loop, or “data flywheel,” where the data generated from its interactions is fed into the system to enhance models. This ability to adapt and become more effective over time offers businesses a powerful tool for driving better decision-making and operational efficiency.






A software engineer who designs, builds, and operates production AI agent systems. This involves creating reliable, multi-step autonomous systems that can reason, plan, use tools, maintain state, and recover from errors, typically through iterative cycles of building, evaluating, observing, and refining non-deterministic LLM-based workflows.





The layered set of models, harnesses, tools, memory, orchestration, and governance required to make AI agents reliable and controllable in real work. Mastering this stack is essential for moving from isolated prompts to robust, self-directed workflows that integrate seamlessly with local hardware and custom system administration tools.





is a hypothetical AI system that possesses the ability to understand, learn, and apply knowledge across a wide range of tasks and domains, similar to human intelligence. AGI aims to replicate the general cognitive abilities of humans, such as reasoning, problem-solving, and creativity, in an artificial system. Achieving AGI is a long-term goal of AI research and development.





is a branch of computer science that focuses on creating intelligent machines that can perform tasks that typically require human intelligence. AI encompasses a wide range of techniques, including machine learning, natural language processing, computer vision, and robotics, to develop systems that can perceive, reason, learn, and act autonomously.





refers to the process of ensuring that AI systems are designed and deployed in a way that aligns with human values, ethical principles, and societal norms. Alignment involves considering the impact of AI systems on various stakeholders, including users, employees, and society as a whole. By aligning AI systems with human values, organizations can build trust, promote fairness, and mitigate potential risks associated with AI technologies.





is a type of AI model that generates text one token (word or character) at a time, with each token being predicted based on the previous ones. This means the model uses its own generated output as part of the input for predicting the next token, creating a sequence that builds on itself. A well-known example of an auto-regressive language model is GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer). These models are trained on large datasets and learn to predict the next word in a sentence, making them capable of generating coherent and contextually relevant text.





A key component in neural networks that helps models focus on relevant parts of input data. The attention mechanism allows the model to assign different weights to different parts of the input, enabling it to learn which elements are more important for the task at hand. This mechanism has been widely used in various deep learning architectures, such as transformers, to improve performance in tasks like machine translation, image captioning, and text summarization.

Perception: AI agents gather and process data from various sources, such as sensors, databases and digital interfaces. This involves extracting meaningful features, recognizing objects or identifying relevant entities in the environment.
Reasoning: A large language model acts as the orchestrator, or reasoning engine, that understands tasks, generates solutions and coordinates specialized models for specific functions like content creation, visual processing or recommendation systems. This step uses techniques like retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to access proprietary data sources and deliver accurate, relevant outputs.
Action: By integrating with external tools and software via application programming interfaces, agentic AI can quickly execute tasks based on the plans it has formulated. Guardrails can be built into AI agents to help ensure they execute tasks correctly. For example, a customer service AI agent may be able to process claims up to a certain amount, while claims above the amount would have to be approved by a human.
Learning: Agentic AI continuously improves through a feedback loop, or “data flywheel,” where the data generated from its interactions is fed into the system to enhance models. This ability to adapt and become more effective over time offers businesses a powerful tool for driving better decision-making and operational efficiency.






A software engineer who designs, builds, and operates production AI agent systems. This involves creating reliable, multi-step autonomous systems that can reason, plan, use tools, maintain state, and recover from errors, typically through iterative cycles of building, evaluating, observing, and refining non-deterministic LLM-based workflows.





The layered set of models, harnesses, tools, memory, orchestration, and governance required to make AI agents reliable and controllable in real work. Mastering this stack is essential for moving from isolated prompts to robust, self-directed workflows that integrate seamlessly with local hardware and custom system administration tools.





is a hypothetical AI system that possesses the ability to understand, learn, and apply knowledge across a wide range of tasks and domains, similar to human intelligence. AGI aims to replicate the general cognitive abilities of humans, such as reasoning, problem-solving, and creativity, in an artificial system. Achieving AGI is a long-term goal of AI research and development.





is a branch of computer science that focuses on creating intelligent machines that can perform tasks that typically require human intelligence. AI encompasses a wide range of techniques, including machine learning, natural language processing, computer vision, and robotics, to develop systems that can perceive, reason, learn, and act autonomously.





refers to the process of ensuring that AI systems are designed and deployed in a way that aligns with human values, ethical principles, and societal norms. Alignment involves considering the impact of AI systems on various stakeholders, including users, employees, and society as a whole. By aligning AI systems with human values, organizations can build trust, promote fairness, and mitigate potential risks associated with AI technologies.





is a type of AI model that generates text one token (word or character) at a time, with each token being predicted based on the previous ones. This means the model uses its own generated output as part of the input for predicting the next token, creating a sequence that builds on itself. A well-known example of an auto-regressive language model is GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer). These models are trained on large datasets and learn to predict the next word in a sentence, making them capable of generating coherent and contextually relevant text.





A key component in neural networks that helps models focus on relevant parts of input data. The attention mechanism allows the model to assign different weights to different parts of the input, enabling it to learn which elements are more important for the task at hand. This mechanism has been widely used in various deep learning architectures, such as transformers, to improve performance in tasks like machine translation, image captioning, and text summarization.

title: Glossary
text:
B

Backpropagation

is a fundamental algorithm in the training of artificial neural networks. It is used to update the weights of the network in order to minimize the error between the predicted output and the actual output. Backpropagation works by calculating the gradient of the loss function with respect to each weight in the network, and then using this gradient to update the weights in the direction that reduces the error. This process is repeated iteratively until the network converges to a set of weights that minimize the error.



Bagging

is an ensemble learning technique that combines multiple models to improve predictive performance. Bagging, short for bootstrap aggregating, involves training each model on a random subset of the training data with replacement. The final prediction is made by aggregating the predictions of all models, such as taking the average for regression tasks or voting for classification tasks. Bagging helps reduce overfitting and improve the stability and accuracy of the model.



Bayesian Optimization

is a technique used in machine learning to optimize hyperparameters of a model by modeling the objective function as a probabilistic surrogate. Bayesian optimization uses a probabilistic model, such as Gaussian processes, to model the objective function and guide the search for optimal hyperparameters. By iteratively evaluating the objective function and updating the probabilistic model, Bayesian optimization efficiently finds the best hyperparameters for the model.



Benchmark

is a standardized test or evaluation procedure used to compare the performance of different machine learning models on a specific task or dataset. Benchmarks provide a common framework for researchers and developers to assess the capabilities of different models, identify state-of-the-art approaches, and track progress in the field. Common benchmarks include image classification tasks, natural language processing tasks, and reinforcement learning environments. List of benchmarks.



(BERT) Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

is a pre-trained language model developed by Google that uses a transformer architecture to learn bidirectional representations of text. BERT is trained on a large corpus of text data using unsupervised learning, allowing it to capture deep contextual relationships between words and phrases. BERT has been widely adopted in natural language processing tasks, such as question answering, text classification, and named entity recognition, due to its ability to generate high-quality contextual embeddings.



(BM25) Best Matching 25

is a classic and widely used sparse retrieval model for information retrieval tasks. Unlike dense embedding models like DPR, which rely on dense vector representations, BM25 is based on lexical matching and statistical properties of text. It is a probabilistic model that ranks documents or passages based on their relevance to a query. BM25 is commonly used in search engines and information retrieval systems to retrieve relevant documents or passages based on keyword matching and term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) weighting. BM25 remains a popular choice for retrieval tasks due to its simplicity, efficiency, and strong performance in many scenarios. However, for tasks requiring semantic understanding, dense embedding models like DPR are often preferred.


Key Features of BM25:

Sparse Representation:
BM25 operates on the bag-of-words assumption, where documents and queries are represented as sparse vectors of term frequencies. It does not capture semantic meaning but relies on exact keyword matching.
Term Frequency and Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF):
BM25 combines term frequency (TF) (how often a term appears in a document) and inverse document frequency (IDF) (how rare or common a term is across the entire corpus) to compute relevance scores.
Tunable Parameters:
BM25 has two key parameters:
k₁: Controls the saturation of term frequency (how quickly the influence of repeated terms levels off).
b: Controls the impact of document length normalization (penalizing longer documents).
Efficiency:
BM25 is computationally efficient and works well with inverted indices, making it suitable for large-scale retrieval tasks.



How BM25 Works:

Input:
A query (e.g., “What is the capital of France?”) and a collection of documents or passages.
Tokenization:
The query and documents are tokenized into individual terms.
Scoring:
For each document, BM25 computes a relevance score based on the presence of query terms in the document, their frequencies, and their IDF values.
Ranking:
Documents are ranked by their BM25 scores, and the top-k most relevant documents are returned.



Advantages of BM25:

Simplicity:
BM25 is easy to implement and does not require training data or complex neural networks.
Efficiency:
It is computationally lightweight and works well with inverted indices, making it suitable for large-scale retrieval tasks.
Robustness:
BM25 performs well in many retrieval tasks, especially when exact keyword matching is important.
Interpretability:
The scoring mechanism is transparent and interpretable, unlike dense embedding models.



Limitations of BM25:

Lack of Semantic Understanding:
BM25 relies on exact keyword matching and cannot capture semantic relationships between terms (e.g., synonyms or paraphrases).
Static Scoring:
The model does not adapt to specific domains or tasks unless the parameters (k1k1​, bb) are tuned.
Handling of Long Documents:
While BM25 includes document length normalization, it may still struggle with very long documents or queries.




(BPE) Byte Pair Encoding

is a data compression technique used in natural language processing to tokenize text into subword units. BPE works by iteratively merging the most frequent pairs of characters or subwords in a corpus to create a vocabulary of subword units. This allows the model to represent rare or out-of-vocabulary words as combinations of subword units, improving the generalization and efficiency of the model. BPE is commonly used in transformer-based language models like GPT and BERT to handle rare words and improve the model’s performance on various NLP tasks.



Boosting

is an ensemble learning technique that combines multiple weak learners to create a strong learner. Boosting works by training each model sequentially, where each subsequent model focuses on correcting the errors made by the previous models. The final prediction is made by aggregating the predictions of all models, such as taking a weighted sum of the predictions. Boosting helps improve the accuracy and generalization of the model by reducing bias and variance.

title: Glossary
text:
C

(CLIP) Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining

is a multimodal model developed by OpenAI that learns joint representations of text and images. CLIP is trained on a large dataset of image-text pairs to understand the relationship between visual and textual information. By learning to associate images with their corresponding textual descriptions, CLIP can perform tasks like zero-shot image classification, image generation from text prompts, and multimodal retrieval. CLIP has demonstrated strong performance on various vision-and-language tasks and has been used in applications like content moderation, recommendation systems, and creative AI. CLIP revolutionized AI by bridging vision and language, enabling powerful multimodal applications. It remains a cornerstone for tasks requiring joint understanding of text and images, from search to generative AI.


Key Features:

Multimodal Alignment:
CLIP maps images and text into a shared embedding space, where corresponding image-text pairs are close to each other.
Enables cross-modal tasks like image search using text queries or vice versa.
Zero-Shot Learning:
CLIP can perform tasks like classification, retrieval, or captioning without fine-tuning by leveraging natural language prompts (e.g., “a photo of a dog”).
Contrastive Learning:
Trained using a contrastive loss to maximize similarity between correct image-text pairs and minimize similarity for mismatched pairs.
Large-Scale Training:
Trained on 400 million image-text pairs from the internet, covering diverse concepts and styles.



How CLIP Works:

Dual-Encoder Architecture:
Image Encoder: A vision backbone (e.g., Vision Transformer or ResNet) converts images into embeddings.
Text Encoder: A transformer-based model converts text into embeddings.
Embedding Space:
Images and text are projected into a shared 512-dimensional space.
Similarity between image and text embeddings is measured using cosine similarity.
Zero-Shot Inference:
For classification, generate text embeddings for possible class labels (e.g., “cat,” “dog”) and compare them with the image embedding.
The label with the highest similarity is selected as the prediction.



Applications:

Zero-Shot Image Classification:
Classify images using natural language prompts without task-specific training.
Example: Predict whether an image shows a “golden retriever” or “labrador.”
Image Retrieval:
Search for images using text queries (e.g., “a sunset over mountains”).
Text-Guided Image Generation:
Used with generative models (e.g., DALL·E) to create images from text prompts.
Content Moderation:
Detect inappropriate images or text based on embeddings.
Multimodal Search:
Build systems that retrieve images or text across modalities.



Strengths:

Flexibility: Adapts to new tasks via natural language prompts.
Scalability: Handles diverse concepts due to large-scale training.
Efficiency: No need for labeled data for downstream tasks.



Limitations:

Bias:
Inherits societal biases from web-scale training data
Fine-Grained Understanding:
Struggles with subtle distinctions (e.g., dog breeds or nuanced art styles).
Computational Cost:
Training requires significant resources, though inference is efficient.
Static Knowledge:
Limited to knowledge present in its training data (up to 2021 for CLIP models).



CLIP Variants:

OpenCLIP: Open-source reimplementation of CLIP with community-driven training.
CLIP-ViT: Vision Transformer-based image encoder for improved performance.
CLIP+GAN: Combines CLIP with generative adversarial networks (e.g., StyleCLIP).
